claim: Standard mixed-precision training stores 6 bytes of weights (fp32 master plus fp16 copy), 4 bytes of fp32 gradient and 8 bytes of Adam state per parameter, so a fully trainable model costs at least 18 bytes per parameter before activations.
stance_target: The repo's memory arithmetic that 7B fully trainable with Adam needs ~112 GB per card
scope_conditions: Standard AMP plus Adam; the paper's own accounting section
quoted_support: For each parameter, the components stored on GPU memory are then: the single precision value of the model weight and its half precision copy (6 bytes), the optimizer state (dependent on the optimizer), the gradient (usually 4 bytes), and some additional values like the forward activations whose size may vary depending on the model.

claim: Optimizer state, not weights or gradients, is usually the largest single memory term, consuming up to twice as much memory as the parameters themselves.
stance_target: The repo's diagnosis that Adam state (84 GB for 7B) is what breaks the 64 GB DDP budget
quoted_support: memory requirements for modern model training are often dictated by the optimizer state, with up to twice as much memory required for each parameter.
numbers: up to 2x parameter memory for optimizer state

claim: The fp32 master copy of the weights can be replaced by storing only the residual extra bits between the fp16/bf16 value and its fp32 original, saving at least 6 bytes per parameter without changing hyperparameters or the training framework.
stance_target: The claim that per-parameter memory overhead is reducible below the standard 16-18 byte AMP budget
scope_conditions: Adam and SGD on fp16/bf16 models; DLRM, ResNet-18, T5, DCGAN
quoted_support: For a given parameter, this leads to - at least - 6 bytes less having to remain stored on the memory.

claim: Measured peak-memory reduction is 54% on a synthetic 2B-parameter SGD run (against a stated theoretical maximum of 60%), 11% when fine-tuning T5 on GLUE, and 20-25% in realistic training conditions.
stance_target: How much of the theoretical per-parameter saving survives in practice
scope_conditions: Synthetic 2B model with SGD plus momentum; T5 fine-tuning on GLUE; DLRM, ResNet-18, DCGAN
quoted_support: The results displayed in Figure 2 show we achieve up to 54% lower peak memory use on a sample network compared to a standard mixed-precision training. This is close to the theoretical maximum loss of 60% in this case.

claim: Removing the gradient buffer and fusing the optimizer step into the backward pass yields up to 16% faster training on ResNet-18 and a 2-10% gain from the fused optimizer alone.
stance_target: Whether memory-saving optimizer changes can also improve throughput rather than only cost it
scope_conditions: ResNet-18 image classification; fused versus standard optimizer variants
quoted_support: On actual model training, our solution achieve up to 16% faster training on the Resnet-18 model, as compared to classic mixed-precision training.

claim: Fusing the backward pass with the optimizer step makes gradient accumulation impossible, which disqualifies this technique for any batch plan that reaches a 1M-token global batch by accumulating micro-batches.
stance_target: The repo's plan of 6 gradient-accumulation steps of 32k tokens to reach a 1M-token global batch, if combined with fused optimizer steps
scope_conditions: Any implementation that steps the optimizer during backpropagation; stated as a hard limitation by the authors
quoted_support: The use of gradient accumulation (stepping the optimizer after several back-propagation) therefore becomes impossible.

claim: Fusing backward with the optimizer step also removes the interval where gradient clipping and loss scaling normally run, so both must be reimplemented as parameter hooks or the training becomes unstable.
stance_target: The operational cost of adopting fused optimizer steps on a bf16 training run
scope_conditions: Gradient clipping and loss scaling applied between backward and optimizer step
quoted_support: Gradient clipping is a method designed to prevent exploding gradients by setting a threshold on their values. It is usually applied between the backward pass and the optimizer step, it then becomes impossible when both are fused.

claim: The extra-bits scheme trades accuracy for memory: storing only the leading bits of the fp32 significand is equivalent to round-to-zero, which is less accurate than the round-to-nearest used by standard mixed precision.
stance_target: The assumption that the technique is accuracy-neutral relative to standard AMP
scope_conditions: 16-bit compute values reconstructed from truncated fp32 significands
quoted_support: saving only the first part of the 32bit significand is equivalent to applying a round-to-zero operation on the full precision value, which is known to be less accurate than the standard round-to-nearest used in this case.

claim: The paper's own comparison fixes the optimizer-state ladder at 8 bytes per parameter for Adam, 4 for Adafactor and 2 for 8-bit Adam, which is the same ladder the repo's 112 GB figure depends on.
stance_target: The repo's use of 12 bytes of optimizer state (fp32 m, fp32 v, fp32 master) as the Adam baseline
scope_conditions: Adam-family optimizers; byte counts per parameter
quoted_support: Where a standard Adam optimizer would require 8 bytes of state memory by parameter, these optimizers respectively uses 4 bytes and 2 bytes only.
